records.text: He was a Jewish man living in the city of Susa, a great man serving in the king’s court.
records.prior_reason: The introductory court residence and high standing do not establish a distinct particular connection beyond the same recurring character; no generic court-service link is retained.

records.text: This was his dream: Look! Voices and tumult, thunders and an earthquake, disturbance upon the earth!
records.prior_reason: The dream's voices, tumult, thunder and earthquake are not matched to a separately narrated literal earthquake or an unrelated cosmic-judgment text.

records.text: Look! A day of darkness and gloom, affliction and distress, suffering and great disturbance upon the earth!
records.prior_reason: The dream's darkness and distress are preserved; a generic darkness or tribulation analogy would not establish a particular additional target for this unit.

records.text: Mordecai stayed quietly in the court with Gabatha and Tharra, the king’s two eunuchs who guarded the court.
records.prior_reason: The court companions are named Gabatha and Tharra, but the later eunuch notices do not supply those names. No individual equation is retained solely from their court role.

records.text: The king ordered Mordecai to serve in the court and gave him gifts for these things.
records.prior_reason: The opening explicitly gives Mordecai court service and gifts, whereas the later reward inquiry reports none. Their precise reward chronology is unresolved; no invented harmonization is retained.

records.text: in those very days, when King Artaxerxes was enthroned in the city of Susa,
records.prior_reason: Susa as the royal seat is a setting notice; no separate event or location identity beyond the same narrative setting supplies a sufficiently particular connection here.

records.text: in the third year of his reign he held a reception for his friends and the other nations, the nobles of Persia and Media, and the rulers of the satraps.
records.prior_reason: The third-year reception and its invited groups are not equated with another royal banquet or an external Artaxerxes chronology.

records.text: After these things, after he had shown them the wealth of his kingdom and the glory of the rejoicing in his wealth for a hundred and eighty days,
records.prior_reason: The 180-day display of wealth is not merged with another feast's duration or treated as a verified date interval for later events.

records.text: when the days of the wedding were completed, the king held a drinking feast for the nations present in the city for six days, in the court of the king’s house,
records.prior_reason: The six-day drinking feast after wedding days is not identified with Esther's later seven-day marriage feast; the particular wedding is not supplied beyond this source.

records.text: which was adorned with fine linen and cotton cloths stretched on fine linen and purple cords upon gold and silver blocks, upon pillars of Parian marble and stone. There were gold and silver couches on a pavement of emerald stone, pearly stone, and Parian stone, and transparent coverings adorned with varied flowers, with roses scattered all around.
records.prior_reason: The detailed textiles, stones, couches and flowers are not made identical to furnishings in another royal or sanctuary scene merely by similar materials.

records.text: There were gold and silver drinking vessels and a garnet cup set out, reckoned at thirty thousand talents. There was abundant sweet wine, which the king himself drank.
records.prior_reason: The precious vessels, garnet cup and abundant wine do not securely identify vessels or a numbered treasury value elsewhere; generic royal drinking is insufficient.

records.text: This drinking feast did not take place according to an established law; rather, the king wished it so and ordered the stewards to carry out his will and that of the people.
records.prior_reason: The absence of an established law for this feast is a particular administrative detail, not a statement that every later royal procedure lacks law.

records.text: Queen Astin also held a drinking feast for the women in the royal quarters, where King Artaxerxes was.
records.prior_reason: Astin's women's feast is not given an independently established motive for her refusal or identified with Esther's later receptions.

records.text: On the seventh day, when the king had become merry, he told Haman, Bazan, Tharra, Boraze, Zatholtha, Abataza, and Tharaba, the seven eunuchs who attended King Artaxerxes,
records.prior_reason: The Haman in the seven-eunuch list lacks the patronymic and Bougaean designation of Haman son of Hammedatha; the shared name alone does not establish personal identity.

records.text: Arcesaeus, Sarsathaeus, and Malesehar, the rulers of Persia and Media who were nearest the king and sat in the first places beside him, approached him
records.prior_reason: The three named nearby Persian and Median rulers are not identified with a different king's counselors or a seven-member council from another account.

records.text: and reported to him, according to the laws, how Queen Astin must be dealt with, because she had not done what the king commanded through the eunuchs.
records.prior_reason: This summary of deliberation over Astin's refusal does not provide a distinct verified legal counterpart beyond the surrounding proposal and decision.

records.text: (for he had recounted to them the queen’s words and how she had contradicted the king). Just as she contradicted King Artaxerxes,
records.prior_reason: The parenthetical recounting of Astin's words remains in its local argument; no additional speaker identity or unreported wording is supplied.

records.text: The proposal pleased the king and the rulers, and the king did as Muchaeus said.
records.prior_reason: The king's acceptance of Muchaeus's proposal is a brief local response; no additional independent royal decision is equated with it.

records.text: Every day Mordecai walked about the women’s court, watching to see what would happen to Esther.
records.prior_reason: Mordecai's daily watching in the women's court is a particular care notice without an independently matched daily action elsewhere.

records.text: Then she entered the king’s presence. Whatever she requested would be handed over to her to accompany her from the women’s quarters to the royal quarters.
records.prior_reason: The general allowance to request items is not converted into a claim that Esther later asked for nothing; the supplied 2:15 says she disregarded none of the guardian's instructions.

records.text: Esther entered the presence of King Artaxerxes in the twelfth month, which is Adar, in the seventh year of his reign.
records.prior_reason: The twelfth month Adar in the seventh year is retained without replacing it with another edition's month or calculating an unsupported regnal chronology.

records.text: Mordecai was serving in the court.
records.prior_reason: The brief court-service notice repeats Mordecai's setting without a sufficiently meaningful additional relationship beyond identification.

records.text: He came as far as the king’s gate and stood there, for he was not permitted to enter the court wearing sackcloth and ashes.
records.prior_reason: The ban on entering the royal court in sackcloth and ashes is not equated with a sanctuary-access law or a different royal entry restriction.

records.text: Achrathaeus came in and spoke all these words to her.
records.prior_reason: The messenger's delivery of the preceding words is preserved without a generic message-delivery cross-reference.

records.text: Esther said to Achrathaeus, “Go to Mordecai and say:
records.prior_reason: The introduction to Esther's reply does not independently supply a substantive connection beyond the following complete speech.

records.text: Achrathaeus reported all Esther’s words to Mordecai.
records.prior_reason: The messenger's report of Esther's words is a local communication step; no unrelated messenger or court is equated with it.

records.text: Esther sent the man who had come to her back to Mordecai, saying:
records.prior_reason: The return-message introduction is preserved without deriving a separate connection from generic communication.

records.text: Mordecai went and did everything Esther commanded him,
records.prior_reason: Mordecai's carrying out the command is not expanded into additional details about how every participant fasted or assembled.

records.text: and he implored the Lord, remembering all the Lord’s works, and said:
records.prior_reason: The prayer introduction remembers the Lord's works without specifying an individual work in this unit; generic prayer or remembrance parallels are not retained.

records.text: and to open the mouth of nations to praise worthless things, and that a king of flesh might be admired for ever.
records.prior_reason: The feared praise of worthless things and admiration of a mortal king are not equated with another ruler's particular idol or decree.

records.text: But rescue us by Thy hand, and help me, who am alone and have no one except Thee, Lord.
records.prior_reason: The repeated appeal for the Lord's hand and help is preserved without making repetition of a prayer formula alone an additional completed connection.

records.text: While she was speaking, she fell in her faintness. The king was troubled, and all his attendants comforted her.
records.prior_reason: The renewed faintness and comfort by the attendants belong to the complete approach scene, but no additional particular independent connection is selected for this repeated physical reaction.

records.text: The king said, “Hurry Haman here, so that we may carry out Esther’s word.” Both came to the reception Esther had spoken of.
records.prior_reason: The arrival of the invited king and Haman is already the concrete target for the invitation link; no additional substantive comparison is selected for this transitional fulfillment unit.

records.text: She said, “My request and my petition are this:
records.prior_reason: The introductory words my request and my petition are completed in the following unit; the fragment alone supplies no additional particular target.

records.text: The king’s attendants said, “Behold, Haman is standing in the court.” The king said, “Call him.”
records.prior_reason: The attendants identify Haman in the court and the king summons him; this transition has no additional distinctive connection beyond the execution-request scene already retained.

records.text: He said to the king, “As for a man whom the king wishes to honor,
records.prior_reason: The unfinished introduction to the honored man is completed in the following proposal; no independent target is selected for the introductory fragment.

records.text: The king said, “Who is this who dared to do this deed?”
records.prior_reason: The question asking who dared the deed introduces the identification of Haman; the question alone does not supply a further substantive comparison.

records.text: The following is a copy of the letter:
records.prior_reason: This unit only introduces the copy of the letter; the letter heading and particular provisions are reviewed in their own actual source units.

records.text: They not only abolish gratitude among people, but, lifted up by the boasts of those unacquainted with goodness, they suppose they will escape the evil-hating justice of God, Who always watches over all things.
records.prior_reason: The general reflection on ingratitude and imagined escape from divine justice has no separately selected particular target beyond generic moral resemblance.

records.text: For he thought that by these means he could find us isolated and transfer the rule of the Persians to the Macedonians.
records.prior_reason: The accusation that Haman intended to transfer Persian rule to Macedonians is the letter's particular allegation; no independent narrative confirmation or external identity is established for it.

records.text: Every city or region, without exception, that does not act according to these instructions will be consumed in wrath by spear and fire. It will be made not only impassable to human beings but also most hateful to wild beasts and birds for all time.
records.prior_reason: The precise sanction of spear, fire and permanent desolation for noncomplying regions is not linked to unrelated destruction or curse passages merely because their imagery overlaps.

records.text: and Pharsannestain, Delphon, Phasga,
records.prior_reason: Pharsannestain, Delphon and Phasga are preserved as names in the sons list; no individually distinguishing cross-text identities have been established.

records.text: Phardatha, Barea, Sarbacha,
records.prior_reason: Phardatha, Barea and Sarbacha are preserved as actual names in the sons list; no independent person-level comparison has been established.

records.text: Marmasima, Arouphaion, Arsaion, and Zabouthaithan,
records.prior_reason: Marmasima, Arouphaion, Arsaion and Zabouthaithan are not equated with other names or reconstructed forms without distinguishing evidence.

records.text: On that very day the number of those who had perished in Susa was delivered to the king.
records.prior_reason: The delivery of the Susa casualty report is necessary context for the retained tally links; no additional substantive target is selected for the administrative transition itself.

records.text: Mordecai and Queen Esther established these things for themselves, against themselves, and then also set their plan against their own health.
records.prior_reason: The actual wording about establishing things against themselves and setting their plan against their own health is not silently replaced by a familiar fasting formulation; the separately read fasting proposal remains unresolved.

records.text: The king set down taxes upon the kingdom, both on land and on sea.
records.prior_reason: The land-and-sea tax notice supplies no specific amount, purpose or matched levy; a generic link to imperial taxation is insufficient.

records.text: His strength and courage, and the wealth and glory of his kingdom—behold, they are written in the book of the kings of the Persians and Medes for a remembrance.
records.prior_reason: The reference to the Persian and Median kings' memorial book does not identify a separately available passage in that record; generic royal wealth or annals formulas are insufficient.

records.text: In the fourth year of the reign of Ptolemy and Cleopatra, Dositheus, who said he was a priest and a Levite, and Ptolemy his son brought in the preceding letter about Phrourai. They said it was authentic and had been translated by Lysimachus son of Ptolemy, one of those in Jerusalem.
records.prior_reason: The colophon's Dositheus, his son Ptolemy, translator Lysimachus and Ptolemy-Cleopatra dating are not assigned identities from common names or an unverified regnal reconstruction.
